tagline: The fourth Gospel: the story of Jesus told as the eternal Word made flesh, written so that readers may believe and have life in his name.
overview:
John is the fourth of the four Gospels, the books that tell the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. It covers the same ground as Matthew, Mark, and Luke, from John the Baptist to the empty tomb, but it tells the story from a different height. Before Jesus is born in Bethlehem or baptized in the Jordan, John takes the reader back to the beginning of everything and names Jesus as the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, who then became flesh and lived among us.

The first half of the book (chapters 1 to 12) is built around a series of signs, miracles that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is: water turned to wine, a boy healed at a distance, a man lame for thirty-eight years made to walk, five thousand fed, a man born blind given sight, and Lazarus raised from the dead. Around the signs come long conversations and arguments, with Nicodemus at night, a Samaritan woman at a well, and crowds and leaders at the Jerusalem feasts. The second half (chapters 13 to 21) slows almost to a stop. Five chapters are given to one evening, Jesus' last meal with his disciples, where he washes their feet, promises the Holy Spirit, and prays for them. Then come the arrest, the trial before Pilate, the crucifixion, the empty tomb, and the risen Jesus meeting Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and Peter.

The book matters because it says most plainly what the other Gospels also claim: that in Jesus the God of Israel has come in person. It is also one of the simplest books in the New Testament to read and one of the deepest to study. Its vocabulary is small (light, life, truth, love, world, believe, abide, glory) and its thought is inexhaustible. Many people have come to faith by reading it first, and it says openly that this is why it was written (20:31).
author:
The Gospel does not name its author. Its closing verses point to a figure it calls the disciple whom Jesus loved, who reclines beside Jesus at the Last Supper (13:23), stands at the cross (19:26), runs to the empty tomb (20:2-8), and is identified as the witness behind the book: “This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.” (21:24). The we in that verse suggests that others around the witness helped bring the book to its final form.

From the late second century the church identified this disciple as John the son of Zebedee, one of the Twelve and the brother of James. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around AD 180, said that John the disciple of the Lord, who leaned on his breast, published the Gospel while living at Ephesus, and Irenaeus claimed a link to that generation through Polycarp of Smyrna. Many scholars still hold this view, pointing to the author's detailed knowledge of Jerusalem and Palestinian geography and to the curious fact that John son of Zebedee is never named in the Gospel.

Others think the beloved disciple was a follower of Jesus who was not one of the Twelve, perhaps a Jerusalem disciple, which would explain his access to the high priest's house (18:15-16). Papias, an early second-century bishop whose words survive through the historian Eusebius, mentions a John the Elder, and some (Richard Bauckham among them) identify the beloved disciple with this elder rather than with the son of Zebedee. A third approach, influential in the second half of the twentieth century and associated with Raymond Brown and J. Louis Martyn, reads the Gospel as the product of a Johannine community, a circle of churches shaped by the beloved disciple's testimony, whose own experience (including conflict with synagogue leaders) left its mark on the text as it was written and revised in stages. These views overlap more than they seem: nearly all agree that the book rests on the testimony of a remembered eyewitness and that it came to its final form among his followers.
date: Most scholars date the Gospel to the last decades of the first century, commonly the 90s, and many place it around AD 90 to 100. The reasons are the book's developed reflection on who Jesus is, its references to believers being put out of the synagogue (9:22, 12:42, 16:2), which many read as reflecting a time after the Jewish revolt and the fall of the temple in AD 70, and the early tradition that John wrote last of the four and lived into old age at Ephesus. The latest likely date is set by a small papyrus fragment of John 18, held in the John Rylands Library in Manchester and known as P52, which is usually dated to the first half of the second century, though the exact dating of such fragments is debated. A minority of scholars, including John A. T. Robinson, argued for a date before AD 70, noting that John 5:2 describes a pool in Jerusalem in the present tense and that the Gospel never mentions the temple's destruction.
setting:
The story is set in Judea, Samaria, and Galilee under Roman rule in the late 20s and early 30s AD. Herod the Great's temple, still being expanded, dominated Jerusalem. The high priests Annas and his son-in-law Caiaphas led the temple establishment, and Pontius Pilate governed Judea for Rome from AD 26 to 36. John is unusually attentive to the Jewish festivals: several Passovers (2:13, 6:4, 11:55), the Feast of Tabernacles (chapter 7), and the Feast of Dedication, now called Hanukkah (10:22). Much of the action takes place in Jerusalem, and the book knows its places well, from the pool of Bethesda to the Stone Pavement where Pilate sat in judgment.

The first readers lived a generation or more later, probably in and around Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey), if the early tradition is right. They were likely a mixed group of Jewish and Gentile believers. The Gospel explains Jewish customs and translates Aramaic words such as Rabbi and Messiah, which suggests that not every reader knew them. It also shows signs of a painful separation between the followers of Jesus and the synagogue. When the Gospel speaks of the Jews, it often means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole: Jesus and all his first disciples were Jews, and Jesus himself says that salvation is from the Jews (4:22).
purpose: John states his purpose plainly near the end: “But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” (20:31). The manuscripts differ slightly in the tense of the verb believe, and scholars debate whether the book was written mainly to bring outsiders to faith or to strengthen believers to keep believing. Both purposes fit the book, which has served as an evangelistic Gospel and as a book for the church's own deepening. It also answers the questions of a community under pressure: who Jesus really is, why his own people largely rejected him, what happens to his followers now that he has returned to the Father, and how they are to live in love for one another while the world hates them.
story: John opens with the first words of Genesis, “In the beginning”, and so places the story of Jesus at the start of everything, as the Word through whom the world was made. It then walks through the story of Israel in a new key: Jesus is the tabernacle where God's glory dwells (1:14), the new temple (2:21), the true bread from heaven given in the wilderness (chapter 6), the light and water of the Feast of Tabernacles (chapters 7 and 8), the good shepherd Ezekiel promised (chapter 10), and the Passover lamb (1:29, 19:36). The Gospel ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples as the Father sent him and breathing the Spirit on them (20:21-22). The story continues in Acts, in the letters of John, and in Revelation, which the church has long associated with the same circle.
christ: Every Gospel is about Jesus, but John makes his identity the explicit subject of nearly every page. He is the Word who was God (1:1), the one and only Son who has made the Father known (1:18), the Lamb of God (1:29), and the Son of Man on whom heaven opens (1:51). Seven times he says I am with a picture attached: “I am the bread of life” (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the gate for the sheep (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25), “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6), and the true vine (15:1). Elsewhere he says I am with nothing after it, most strikingly “before Abraham was born, I am” (8:58), words his hearers take as a claim to the divine name, since they pick up stones. Yet John also shows the Son's full humanity more tenderly than any other Gospel: Jesus is tired at a well, weeps at a friend's tomb, and thirsts on the cross. The Word became flesh, and his glory is seen most fully when he is lifted up on the cross.
reading:
Read John slowly and listen for its double meanings. Words like born again or from above (3:3), living water (4:10), and lifted up (3:14, 12:32) carry two senses at once, and characters regularly hear the lower one while Jesus means the higher. Watch the misunderstandings, the signs, the feasts, and the hour that is not yet come and then arrives. Watch the characters too, who often stand for different responses to Jesus: Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the man born blind, Martha and Mary, Thomas, and Peter.

Two cautions help. First, John's language about the Jews has been misused to justify contempt for Jewish people, a grave misreading of a book written largely by and about Jews; the term usually names the Jerusalem authorities in their opposition. Second, the story of the woman caught in adultery (7:53-8:11) is not found in the earliest manuscripts and is printed in brackets in most modern Bibles, though many think it preserves a true memory of Jesus. Readers comparing John with the other Gospels will also notice differences in order and emphasis, such as the temple cleansing near the start rather than the end. Scholars debate whether John knew the other Gospels or wrote independently; either way, John writes with his own purpose and arranges his material to serve it.

structure.title: Prologue: the Word made flesh
structure.summary: A poem-like opening presents Jesus as the eternal Word, the agent of creation, the light rejected by his own and received by those who become children of God, and the one who has made the unseen Father known.

structure.title: First witnesses and first signs
structure.summary: John the Baptist points to Jesus, the first disciples follow, and Jesus turns water into wine, clears the temple, and speaks with Nicodemus and a Samaritan woman before healing an official's son.

structure.title: Signs and conflict at the feasts
structure.summary: At a series of Jewish festivals Jesus heals, feeds the crowds, and declares himself bread, light, and shepherd, while opposition from the Jerusalem authorities hardens.

structure.title: Lazarus raised and the hour arrives
structure.summary: The raising of Lazarus, the greatest sign, leads the council to plot Jesus' death. He is anointed at Bethany, enters Jerusalem, and announces that his hour has come.

structure.title: The farewell at the table
structure.summary: On his last night Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives the new command to love, promises the Holy Spirit, speaks of the vine and branches, and prays for his followers.

structure.title: Arrest, cross, and resurrection
structure.summary: Jesus is arrested, tried before Annas and Pilate, crucified as King of the Jews, and buried. On the third day Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty and the risen Jesus appears to her, to the disciples, and to Thomas.

structure.title: Epilogue by the sea
structure.summary: The risen Jesus provides a great catch of fish in Galilee, restores Peter with a threefold question of love, and speaks of the beloved disciple, whose testimony stands behind the book.

themes.title: Believing and life
themes.body: The verb believe appears in John far more often than in any other Gospel, yet the noun faith never does. For John, believing is an act, a coming to Jesus, receiving him, and continuing in his word. Its result is life, eternal life, which John describes not only as endless existence after death but as a present sharing in the life of God that begins now and is completed in the resurrection.

themes.title: Signs and glory
themes.body: John calls Jesus' miracles signs because they point beyond themselves. Each reveals something of his glory, the visible weight and brightness of God's presence that Israel saw in the tabernacle and temple. The signs provoke both faith and opposition, and the Gospel suggests that faith resting only on miracles is fragile. The fullest display of glory comes, paradoxically, at the cross, when the Son is lifted up.

themes.title: Light and darkness, truth and the world
themes.body: John uses stark pairs: light and darkness, truth and falsehood, above and below, life and death. The world in John is God's creation, loved by him (3:16), but also humanity organized against him. These contrasts are not a dualism of two equal powers; the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. They describe a crisis of decision that Jesus' coming brings.

themes.title: The Father, the Son, and the Spirit
themes.body: No Gospel says more about the relationship between the Father and the Son, who are one (10:30) and yet distinct, the Son sent by the Father and doing only what he sees the Father doing. In the farewell chapters Jesus promises another helper, the Holy Spirit, who will teach, remind, testify, and convict. The later church's doctrine of the Trinity drew heavily on this Gospel.

themes.title: Love and abiding
themes.body: The Father loves the Son, the Son loves his own to the end, and he commands his disciples to love one another as he has loved them. John's word for remaining or abiding describes a continuing, dependent union with Jesus, pictured as branches in a vine. Love for one another is the sign by which the world will know who his disciples are.

keyChapters.why: The prologue presents Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh, and the first witnesses name him Lamb of God, Messiah, and Son of God.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that one must be born from above, and the chapter contains the Bible's most quoted summary of the gospel, John 3:16.
After feeding five thousand, Jesus declares himself the bread of life, and many disciples turn away while Peter confesses that Jesus has the words of eternal life.
Jesus raises Lazarus after declaring himself the resurrection and the life, the sign that sets the plot to kill him in motion.
At his last meal Jesus washes his disciples' feet and gives the new command to love one another as he has loved them.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples, and all who will believe through their word, that they may be one.
The empty tomb, the risen Jesus with Mary Magdalene and Thomas, and the Gospel's statement of its own purpose.
